units.text: In the deepest shadows of St Andrews University library in Scotland, hidden away in a dark, forgotten corner, sits a 16th-century leather tome.
Its cover is cracked, weathered, and blackened by centuries of damp air.
On the inside of the back cover, an artist in the year 1578 drew a picture that makes the heart turn cold.
It depicts a towering, skeletal man with long, gaunt limbs, standing at the edge of a twisting forest.
Veins bulge across his pale, hairless skull, his dark eyes are sunken deep within bone, and beneath the ink is written a single name: Herbert Solomon.
Let us go back to the winter where this nightmare began.
The book chronicles the isolated town of Ettrick, set amidst the bleak moorlands and dense pine forests of southern Scotland.
In the freezing December of 1577, an unspeakable dread settled over the cobblestone streets.
The first to disappear was young Alana Sutherland.
She had dropped her hand-carved doll down an old stone well on the edge of town, and returned at sunset with a hook and rope to retrieve it.
She was never seen again.
Days later, another child vanished while walking an errand just two streets from his home.
By late January, seven children had been torn from existence.
Fear consumed every cottage, turning neighbor against neighbor.
When two more children vanished in mid-February, the desperate town elder demanded a culprit.
In every house and across every church pew, one whisper grew into a deafening roar: Herbert Solomon.
Solomon was an outsider who lived in a small wooden cabin deep within the Ettrick forest.
Ravaged by an unknown wasting disease, his body was emaciated, his skin sheet-white, and he covered his face with a tarnished hat and cloth.
He would watch the village children play from the tree line.
On several occasions, children returned home carrying exquisitely carved wooden dolls and toys—left on tree stumps as gifts from the gentle recluse.
But to fearful parents, this was proof of evil.
On a freezing February night, grief and hatred reached a boiling pitch.
Decreeing Solomon a child-killing abomination, a mob of villagers armed with axes, scythes, and flaming torches marched into the dark forest.
They surrounded his humble cabin and barred the heavy timbers from outside.
Cheering in a frenzy of revenge, they tossed torches onto the dried thatched roof and watched the cabin ignite into a wall of roaring flame.
Solomon's desperate screams echoed through the Scots pines, before fading into the crackle of falling timber.
Satisfied that justice was served, the mob returned home, convinced the curse was lifted.
Yet within days, a suffocating fog descended over Ettrick, and terror returned with a vengeance.
Townsfolk began waking in the dead of night to the sound of floorboards creaking under an unnatural weight.
An elderly woman woke to rustling beneath her bed, watching in paralyzed horror as a tall, skeletal figure dragged itself across the floor.
In a cellar, a tradesman encountered the gaunt, sheet-white phantom hunched beneath the low rafters.
Then, the impossible occurred: an orphan girl was snatched screaming from the foggy cobblestones.
Days later, another child vanished from his bedroom.
Even inside the parish church, Solomon's tall, spindly shadow stepped into the aisle before dissolving into mist.

Believing Solomon's vengeful wraith had returned to punish the town, Vicar McKenzie assembled a group of chosen men armed with blessed steel, flaming torches, and vials of holy water to hunt the phantom down.
They waited in the midnight mist until the solitary figure of Herbert Solomon appeared, walking the cobblestones with purposeful strides.
McKenzie and his men encircled the creature, brandishing weapons.
The vicar splashed holy water across the stone, and a torch struck Solomon's sleeve, setting the frayed cloth alight.
But the tall figure broke through the circle, fleeing like a giant spider shadow across the village courtyards.
Pursued by the shouting mob, Solomon sprinted down the main street and ducked into an open cottage doorway.
McKenzie and the villagers burst inside, only to find a weak, trembling young girl lying on the hall floor.
With her last ounce of strength, the child pointed toward the stone stairway and whispered a single word: Below.
The vicar descended with his torch into the cold cellar vault, and the breath caught in his throat.
Chained against the damp stone walls were the missing children—malnourished and terrified, but alive!
And lying motionless upon the stone floor was the true fiend: Tom Sutherland, the father of the very first child who had vanished.
Sutherland had killed his daughter in a drunken rage, and consumed by madness, had stolen the other children.
He was about to execute another captive when Herbert Solomon burst through the cellar door, ending Sutherland's reign of terror to save the innocent.
The town rejoiced, realizing with heavy shame that the gentle recluse they had burned alive was their protector all along.
Yet the story does not end in the 16th century.
Centuries later, while researching the Ettrick tome, I visited a colleague's estate near the Scottish borders.
The following afternoon, panicked screams shattered the tranquil countryside—my friend's little daughter had fallen into a violent, swollen river.
Swept by torrential currents toward jagged rocks, the child lost her grip on a slippery tree root.
We plunged into the rapids, but we were too far away.
She was seconds from drowning.
Suddenly, the forest branches cracked.
From the opposite bank, a tall, gaunt figure burst forth at superhuman speed.
A long, skeletal hand plunged deep into the churning foam, pulling the girl gently to safety.
The pale, withered man placed the child on the grass, gazed across the river with dark, sorrowful eyes, and vanished into the Scots pines.
Even in death, Herbert Solomon was the kindest and gentlest of souls.
This story was adapted from Scottish folklore and the legend of Herbert Solomon.
Now tell me.
Would you have judged him by his face?
